stem: Which of the following patients can safely receive non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)?

options.text: Tom, a 10 year old post-op appendicectomy with a history of severe asthma
Anne, a 5 year old with a traumatic radial fracture.
Emily, an 8 year old with septic arthritis, febrile, generally unwell and refusing to eat, on IV antibiotics.
Joshua, a 12 year old with abdominal pain and diarrhea
Jessica, an 18 year old with headache and a history of gastric ulcers.

explanation: NSAIDs are generally appropriate for short-term analgesia in otherwise stable children without major contraindications. A straightforward traumatic fracture is a suitable scenario. Severe asthma, dehydration/poor oral intake with systemic illness, abdominal pain with diarrhoea, and a history of peptic ulcer disease all raise concern for NSAID-related harm or reduced safety.
rationale: This is a safety-focused analgesia question. The best answer is the child with an uncomplicated fracture, as the others have common contraindications or cautions for NSAID use.

optionExplanations.A: Severe asthma can be worsened by NSAIDs in aspirin-sensitive patients.
optionExplanations.B: A traumatic fracture in an otherwise well child is an appropriate indication for NSAID analgesia.
optionExplanations.C: A febrile, unwell child who is not eating may be dehydrated and at higher risk of renal adverse effects from NSAIDs.
optionExplanations.D: Abdominal pain and diarrhoea may indicate gastrointestinal illness and possible dehydration, making NSAIDs less suitable.
optionExplanations.E: A history of gastric ulcers is a contraindication/caution because NSAIDs increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding and ulcer recurrence.
